title: Use the mind's hidden shortcuts as design material.
dek: In Chapter 4 of Rory Sutherland's Alchemy, subconscious hacking shows how placebos, rituals, and symbolic choices can change experience by working with the mind's hidden systems.

marginNote.label: Apprenticeship Note
marginNote.body: When a choice looks irrational, ask what hidden system it is helping the person manage. Design for that system deliberately, then test whether the intervention changes experience or behaviour.

canon.heading: Design for the mind that actually makes the choice.
canon.standfirst: Read Chapter 4, "Subconscious Hacking: Signalling to Ourselves," from Rory Sutherland's Alchemy on PDF pages 169-192. Study how placebos, rituals, and symbolic choices alter experience and behaviour, then stop before Chapter 5.
canon.readerIntro: Read this chapter as a study of the hidden systems people use to interpret and regulate experience. Mark where a placebo, ritual, or symbolic action changes expectation, attention, or behaviour without changing the underlying physical facts. Then audit one product or service: name the hidden job, the current cue, and one intervention that could support it without deception. Stop at PDF page 192.

blocks.label: 01 / Find the hidden job
paragraphs: A choice can perform a psychological job that is invisible in a purely functional description. Start by asking what reassurance, control, identity, or meaning the person is seeking.
Notice which apparently irrational behaviours become sensible once the hidden job is included in the model.

blocks.label: 02 / Study the placebo mechanism
paragraphs: Placebo effects show that expectation and interpretation can change experienced outcomes even when the physical intervention is held constant.
Mark the cues that make an intervention feel credible, active, safe, or worth attending to.

blocks.label: 03 / Separate hacking from deception
paragraphs: A useful psychological intervention works with a real human response; it does not require the designer to make a false claim about what happened.
Ask where a ritual or signal helps people access a beneficial state and where it merely exploits attention without delivering value.

blocks.label: 04 / Design one supportive intervention
paragraphs: Choose one product, service, or experience. Write the hidden job, the expectation or cue shaping it, and one small intervention that could make the desired behaviour easier.
State what you would measure to distinguish a genuine improvement in experience from a temporary novelty effect.

passageAnchors: Why Aspirin Should Be Reassuringly Expensive
closeReading: What hidden job is each apparently irrational behaviour performing for the person who chooses it?
Which cues make a placebo or ritual credible enough to change expectation and experience?
How does the chapter distinguish a useful intervention from deception or empty theatre?
Where does the conscious explanation of a choice differ from the system that actually produces it?
Choose one offer: what hidden job could you support, what intervention would you test, and what result would count as genuine value?

principle.heading: Treat hidden psychology as part of the product.
principle.body: People do not experience an offer through physical function alone. Expectation, ritual, status, reassurance, and meaning can change what the offer does for them; design these layers honestly and test their effect.
principle.example: A health app could begin a difficult habit with a short, consistent ritual that signals care and readiness. The ritual does not pretend to provide treatment; it helps the user enter the state in which the useful behaviour is easier to begin.
principle.practice: Choose one product or service. Write the functional job, the hidden psychological job, the cues currently shaping expectation, and one honest intervention. Name one behavioural measure and one experience measure you would use to test it.

output.heading: Design for the whole human response.
output.body: The best intervention may change expectation, attention, or meaning before it changes the underlying thing. Find that leverage carefully, then prove that it helps.

signals.heading: Four current signals on designing the cues, rituals, and systems that shape experience.

fieldNotes.title: Google gives hard work a distinct model identity
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Google made Gemini 4 Carbon available for complex, multi-step coding, cybersecurity, scientific reasoning, and other long-horizon agentic workflows, while positioning Argon as the choice for most ordinary work.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The model name and the explicit division of labor are cues that help people decide when to invoke deeper reasoning. The product is not only a capability; it is also a mental shortcut for matching task difficulty to the right mode of work.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether users actually route difficult, verification-heavy work to Carbon, or whether the distinction remains launch language without becoming a durable workflow habit.

fieldNotes.title: Apple turns accessibility into a discoverable viewing ritual
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Apple announced a Sign Language option for supported Apple TV titles, designed and tested with Deaf and native signers, with an icon, settings control, and searchable collection to make the feature findable.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The value is carried by more than the underlying interpretation: a label, a setting, and a dedicated collection turn an inclusive capability into a clear expectation users can act on. The cue reduces the work of discovering whether a story is truly available to them.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether the icon and search language become trusted signals of a consistent experience across titles, rather than a promise whose availability is hard to verify.

fieldNotes.title: Maybelline updates a familiar phrase as perceptions change
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Marketing Dive reported that Maybelline is updating its long-running “Maybe she’s born with it. Maybe it’s Maybelline.” line as beauty perceptions evolve, with a punctuation and phrasing change intended to feel more inclusive and empowering.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: A small verbal change can alter the psychological job of a famous line: from explaining beauty as an innate condition to making the brand feel more aligned with present-day agency and self-definition. Familiarity becomes design material rather than a reason to freeze the message.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether the revised line preserves the memory structure that made the original valuable while changing the interpretation people carry into the product experience.

fieldNotes.title: Holiday shoppers want AI help without surrendering the choice
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Retail Dive reported that holiday shoppers are using AI for price comparisons and narrowing gift ideas, while still wanting autonomy in the buying process.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The useful intervention is not maximum automation. A recommendation system can provide reassurance and reduce search effort while preserving the ritual of choosing, which is part of the emotional value of gifting and the buyer’s sense of agency.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether commerce assistants make the next decision easier without making the shopper feel displaced, rushed, or unable to inspect the reasoning behind a suggestion.

tweets.author: TBPN
tweets.title: A startup wins when the new physics force a new story
tweets.summary: This is worth keeping because it treats narrative as part of the operating system, not decoration. A strange technical or market bet has to become desirable before incumbents copy it, and the company has to keep moving fast enough that the story remains attached to real progress.
tweets.text:
With Jensen potentially out, what's in store for NVIDIA and the broader AI ecosystem? So much of NVIDIA's moat was Jensen's incredible tenacity and work ethic. And his dealmaking. The Jensen discount that the market would put on the company would probably be extreme.

In the private markets, a lot of VCs just assumed Jensen would backstop any AI startup above a certain size. There are a ton of neolabs that have raised ~$1B. And many were probably hoping that if they just showed they were on the path to making something commercially viable, they could count on NVIDIA as a backstop.

We've gotten into this period where capital is the primary constraint to the buildout. If one of the biggest financiers of that buildout is potentially gone, the AI sector would be due for a major reckoning.
